subject: C
topic: Indus Water Treaty & Impact on Economy

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Indus Waters Treaty was signed between India and Pakistan in which year?
questions.explanation: The Indus Waters Treaty was signed on 19 September 1960 in Karachi. 1958 is when negotiations were intensified but the treaty wasn't signed. 1962 is the year of the India-China war, unrelated to this treaty. 1965 is the year of the second India-Pakistan war.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Indus Waters Treaty was brokered by which international organization?
questions.explanation: The World Bank (then International Bank for Reconstruction and Development) brokered and mediated the treaty between India and Pakistan. The United Nations was not the mediator though it is involved in international disputes. The ICJ is a judicial body, not a treaty mediator. The ADB was not involved in this treaty.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the Indus Waters Treaty:

(i) The treaty allocates three eastern rivers to India and three western rivers to Pakistan.
(ii) The eastern rivers allocated to India are Sutlej, Beas, and Ravi.
(iii) The western rivers allocated to Pakistan are Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab.
(iv) India has unrestricted use of all six rivers for hydroelectric purposes.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — the treaty divides the six rivers into two groups. (ii) is correct — Sutlej, Beas, and Ravi are the eastern rivers allocated to India. (iii) is correct — Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab are the western rivers allocated to Pakistan. (iv) is wrong — India has limited rights on western rivers; it can use them for hydroelectric power with certain restrictions (run-of-the-river projects only, with limited storage).

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The Indus Waters Treaty significantly affects the hydroelectric power potential of Jammu & Kashmir.
Reason (R): The Jhelum and Chenab rivers, which flow through J&K, are allocated to Pakistan under the treaty, limiting India's storage rights on these rivers.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct — the treaty imposes restrictions on how J&K can harness the Jhelum and Chenab for power generation and storage. (R) is correct — the western rivers including Jhelum and Chenab are allocated to Pakistan, with India having only limited use rights. (R) directly explains (A) because the allocation of these J&K rivers to Pakistan is why J&K's hydroelectric potential is constrained.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Match the following rivers with their allocation under the Indus Waters Treaty:

Column I:
(a) Jhelum
(b) Sutlej
(c) Chenab
(d) Beas

Column II:
(i) Eastern river — allocated to India
(ii) Western river — allocated to Pakistan

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Jhelum (a) is a western river allocated to Pakistan (ii). Sutlej (b) is an eastern river allocated to India (i). Chenab (c) is a western river allocated to Pakistan (ii). Beas (d) is an eastern river allocated to India (i). Option 2 reverses Jhelum and Sutlej allocations. Option 3 swaps Chenab and Sutlej. Option 4 reverses all allocations.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: Under the Indus Waters Treaty, India is permitted to use western rivers for which of the following purposes?
options: Only domestic and non-consumptive uses, limited agriculture, and run-of-the-river hydroelectric projects
Complete diversion for irrigation in Punjab
questions.correctAnswer: Only domestic and non-consumptive uses, limited agriculture, and run-of-the-river hydroelectric projects
questions.explanation: India is permitted domestic use, non-consumptive use, limited agricultural use, and run-of-the-river hydroelectric generation on western rivers. 'Unrestricted irrigation and storage' is wrong — storage is severely limited. 'Complete diversion for irrigation in Punjab' is wrong — diversion of western rivers is not allowed. 'No use whatsoever' is wrong — the treaty does allow restricted uses.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Which of the following hydroelectric projects in J&K have been subjects of dispute or objection by Pakistan under the Indus Waters Treaty?

(i) Baglihar Dam
(ii) Kishanganga Project
(iii) Salal Dam
(iv) Dulhasti Project

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) Baglihar Dam on Chenab was objected to by Pakistan and went to a Neutral Expert in 2005. (ii) Kishanganga Project was taken to the Permanent Court of Arbitration by Pakistan. (iii) Salal Dam on Chenab was also disputed and resolved through bilateral talks in 1978. (iv) Dulhasti Project was not a major disputed project under the treaty mechanisms.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Permanent Indus Commission was established under the treaty. In the context of J&K's hydroelectric projects, what is its primary function?
options: To adjudicate all water disputes between India and Pakistan
To serve as a regular communication channel and resolve questions on treaty implementation
To construct dams and canals on the Indus system
To collect revenue from water usage by both countries
questions.correctAnswer: To serve as a regular communication channel and resolve questions on treaty implementation
questions.explanation: The Permanent Indus Commission, with one Commissioner from each country, is the treaty's first-tier mechanism: a standing channel for exchanging data and taking up questions of implementation, including Pakistan's objections to J&K projects such as Baglihar, Kishanganga and Ratle. 'To adjudicate all water disputes' is wrong — unresolved differences escalate to a Neutral Expert or a Court of Arbitration. 'To construct dams and canals' is wrong — it builds nothing. 'To collect revenue from water usage' is wrong — the treaty provides for no such levy.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the impact of the Indus Waters Treaty on J&K's irrigation:

(i) J&K cannot build large storage dams on the Jhelum for irrigation purposes.
(ii) The treaty restricts J&K's capacity to store water for dry-season agriculture.
(iii) The Ravi river flows entirely within J&K, giving the state unrestricted rights.
(iv) Run-of-the-river projects do not allow significant water storage for irrigation.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — large storage dams on western rivers (including Jhelum) are restricted. (ii) is correct — limited storage means insufficient water availability during dry seasons. (iv) is correct — run-of-the-river projects generate power but don't store water for irrigation. (iii) is wrong — the Ravi does NOT flow through J&K (it flows mainly through Himachal Pradesh and Punjab); J&K's main rivers are Jhelum and Chenab.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Baglihar Hydroelectric Power Project is located on which river?
questions.explanation: The Baglihar Dam (Baglihar Hydroelectric Power Project) is built on the Chenab river in the Doda district of J&K. It is not on the Jhelum (which flows through the Kashmir Valley). It is not on the Indus (which flows through Ladakh). The Tawi is a smaller river flowing through Jammu city.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Despite having significant river water resources, J&K faces irrigation deficits in many areas.
Reason (R): The Indus Waters Treaty restricts India's ability to build large storage reservoirs on the Jhelum and Chenab in J&K.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct — J&K paradoxically has abundant river water but insufficient irrigation infrastructure. (R) is correct — treaty restrictions on storage on western rivers limit dam construction for irrigation. (R) explains (A) because the inability to store water due to treaty restrictions is a major reason for irrigation shortfalls in J&K.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Indus Waters Treaty was signed by which Indian Prime Minister on behalf of India?
questions.explanation: The treaty was signed on 19 September 1960 by Indian PM Jawaharlal Nehru and Pakistan President Ayub Khan, in the presence of World Bank President Eugene Black. Lal Bahadur Shastri became PM in 1964. Morarji Desai was PM in 1977-79. Indira Gandhi was PM from 1966.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the dispute resolution mechanism under the Indus Waters Treaty:

(i) The first step is resolution through the Permanent Indus Commission.
(ii) If the PIC fails, a Neutral Expert can be appointed.
(iii) The final step is referral to a Court of Arbitration.
(iv) The United Nations Security Council is the final arbiter.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — the PIC is the first level of dispute resolution. (ii) is correct — a Neutral Expert can be appointed for technical questions. (iii) is correct — a Court of Arbitration (7-member) can be constituted for unresolved disputes. (iv) is wrong — the UNSC is not part of the treaty's dispute resolution mechanism; the treaty has its own three-tier system.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: What is the concept of 'run-of-the-river' hydroelectric projects as permitted by the Indus Waters Treaty?
options: Projects with massive water storage reservoirs behind dams
Projects that use the natural flow of the river without significant storage
Projects that completely divert river water for power generation
Underground hydroelectric projects with no surface structures
questions.correctAnswer: Projects that use the natural flow of the river without significant storage
questions.explanation: Run-of-the-river projects harness the kinetic energy of flowing river water without creating large reservoirs — they have minimal or no water storage. 'Massive storage reservoirs' describes conventional dam projects which are restricted. 'Complete diversion' is not permitted under the treaty. 'Underground projects with no surface structures' does not define run-of-the-river.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Match the following hydroelectric projects in J&K with the rivers they are built on:

Column I:
(a) Uri-I
(b) Baglihar
(c) Kishanganga
(d) Salal

Column II:
(i) Chenab
(ii) Jhelum
(iii) Kishanganga (Neelum)

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Uri-I is on the Jhelum river (ii). Baglihar is on the Chenab river (i). Kishanganga project is on the Kishanganga (Neelum) river (iii). Salal is on the Chenab river (i). Option 2 incorrectly places Uri on Chenab. Option 3 swaps Baglihar and Kishanganga. Option 4 places Uri on Kishanganga.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Kishanganga Hydroelectric Project dispute between India and Pakistan was referred to which body for arbitration?
questions.explanation: Pakistan took the Kishanganga dispute to the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) at The Hague. The ICJ was not approached for this specific case. The Neutral Expert mechanism was used for Baglihar, not Kishanganga. The UN General Assembly does not adjudicate bilateral water disputes.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are economic impacts of the Indus Waters Treaty on J&K?

(i) Restriction on large dam construction limits flood control capacity.
(ii) Limited irrigation storage affects agricultural productivity in dry months.
(iii) J&K cannot generate any hydroelectric power from western rivers.
(iv) The treaty has affected industrialization by limiting reliable water and power supply.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — restricted dam heights and storage limit flood management. (ii) is correct — limited water storage impacts agriculture during dry spells. (iv) is correct — inadequate power and water infrastructure has affected industrial growth. (iii) is wrong — India CAN generate hydroelectric power from western rivers through run-of-the-river projects (like Uri, Baglihar, Salal); it is only large storage that is restricted.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Under the Indus Waters Treaty, India is allowed a maximum water storage of __________ MAF (Million Acre Feet) on the western rivers.
questions.explanation: The treaty permits India a maximum storage capacity of approximately 3.60 MAF on the western rivers for various purposes. 1.25 MAF is too low. 5.80 MAF and 8.00 MAF exceed the actual permitted limit under the treaty provisions.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Indus river system, which drains Ladakh and much of J&K, originates primarily from which geographical region?
questions.explanation: The Indus rises near Lake Mansarovar on the Tibetan Plateau and its major tributaries descend from the Western Himalayas and Karakoram, entering India through Ladakh before the system's western rivers traverse J&K. 'Aravalli Range' is wrong — that ancient range in Rajasthan feeds no part of the Indus system. 'Western Ghats' is wrong — those drain the peninsular west-flowing rivers such as the Periyar. 'Vindhya Range' is wrong — it is the source region of the Narmada and Son, in central India.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The Baglihar Dam was the first project referred to a Neutral Expert under the Indus Waters Treaty.
Reason (R): Pakistan objected to the design features of the dam, particularly its gated spillways and height.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct — Baglihar was indeed the first case where a Neutral Expert (Professor Raymond Lafitte) was appointed under the treaty in 2005. (R) is correct — Pakistan specifically objected to the gated spillways, dam height, and pondage level of Baglihar. (R) explains (A) because Pakistan's specific objections to design features are what led to the unprecedented referral to a Neutral Expert.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the economic significance of the Chenab river for J&K:

(i) Multiple hydroelectric projects on the Chenab provide significant power to J&K.
(ii) The Chenab valley supports agriculture through canal irrigation.
(iii) The river facilitates transport of timber and other goods in hilly areas.
(iv) The Chenab is the longest river flowing through J&K.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — Salal, Baglihar, Dulhasti and other projects on Chenab generate substantial power. (ii) is correct — canal systems in Doda, Kishtwar, and Jammu areas draw from the Chenab. (iii) is correct — traditionally, timber was floated down the Chenab. (iv) is correct — the Chenab, at approximately 1,180 km total length, is the longest river flowing through J&K.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Neutral Expert appointed for the Baglihar Dam dispute gave his decision in which year?
questions.explanation: The Neutral Expert, Professor Raymond Lafitte, gave his final decision on 12 February 2007. 2005 is when the referral was made. 2010 and 2013 relate to Kishanganga arbitration proceedings, not Baglihar.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a restriction imposed on India regarding the western rivers under the Indus Waters Treaty?
options: India cannot build run-of-the-river projects on western rivers
India cannot build storage works beyond prescribed limits
India cannot divert western river waters for irrigation beyond specified limits
India must maintain minimum flow downstream at all times
questions.correctAnswer: India cannot build run-of-the-river projects on western rivers
questions.explanation: India IS permitted to build run-of-the-river hydroelectric projects on western rivers — this is NOT a restriction but rather an allowed use. India cannot build storage beyond limits (correct restriction). India cannot divert for irrigation beyond limits (correct restriction). India must maintain flows downstream (correct obligation).

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the impact of the Indus Waters Treaty on J&K's economy:

(i) J&K has significant untapped hydroelectric potential due to treaty restrictions.
(ii) The treaty was signed without consulting the people of J&K.
(iii) Agricultural land in J&K that could be irrigated remains rain-fed due to storage limits.
(iv) The treaty has no impact on J&K's power generation capacity.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — J&K's hydroelectric potential of approximately 20,000 MW is largely untapped, partly due to treaty constraints. (ii) is correct — the treaty was signed between the central governments; J&K was not a party to the negotiations. (iii) is correct — much cultivable land relies on rain rather than canal irrigation due to storage restrictions. (iv) is wrong — the treaty clearly impacts J&K's power generation by restricting storage-based projects.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The total estimated hydroelectric power potential of J&K is approximately:
questions.explanation: J&K's total estimated hydroelectric potential is approximately 20,000 MW, of which only about 3,500 MW has been harnessed. 5,000 MW is approximately the harnessed capacity. 11,000 MW is the potential of Chenab basin alone. 35,000 MW exceeds the total estimated potential of J&K.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Match the following treaty-related events with their years:

Column I:
(a) Signing of the Indus Waters Treaty
(b) Baglihar Neutral Expert decision
(c) Kishanganga arbitration final award
(d) India placed the treaty in abeyance

Column II:
(i) 2025
(ii) 1960
(iii) 2013
(iv) 2007

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: The treaty was signed in 1960, so (a)-(ii). The Neutral Expert gave his decision on the Baglihar dispute in 2007, so (b)-(iv). The Court of Arbitration issued its final award on Kishanganga in 2013, so (c)-(iii). India announced that it was holding the treaty in abeyance in April 2025, after the Pahalgam attack, so (d)-(i). Every other option misassigns at least two of these pairs, most commonly by swapping the 1960 signing with a later dispute year.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: Which Indian organization is responsible for implementing the Indus Waters Treaty from India's side?
questions.explanation: The Indian Commissioner for Indus Waters, under the Ministry of Jal Shakti (formerly Water Resources), is the designated authority for treaty implementation. The Central Water Commission advises but is not the designated implementer. NWDA deals with inter-linking of rivers. The Ministry of External Affairs handles diplomatic matters but not direct treaty implementation.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the Jhelum river and the treaty:

(i) The Jhelum originates at Verinag in J&K.
(ii) Under the treaty, India can use the Jhelum for run-of-the-river power generation.
(iii) The Uri hydroelectric projects are built on the Jhelum.
(iv) India has unrestricted irrigation rights on the Jhelum.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — the Jhelum originates from Verinag spring in Anantnag district. (ii) is correct — run-of-the-river projects are permitted on western rivers. (iii) is correct — Uri-I (480 MW) and Uri-II (240 MW) are on the Jhelum. (iv) is wrong — India does NOT have unrestricted irrigation rights on western rivers; irrigation use is limited to specified acreage.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Indus Waters Treaty allows India limited agricultural use of western rivers. What is the approximate area India is permitted to irrigate from these rivers?
questions.explanation: The treaty permits India to irrigate approximately 1.34 million acres (about 13.43 lakh acres) from the western rivers. 0.5 million acres is too low. 3.5 million acres and 7 million acres far exceed the permitted limit.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The Kishanganga Hydroelectric Project was allowed to proceed by the Court of Arbitration despite Pakistan's objections.
Reason (R): The court ruled that India could divert water from the Kishanganga river for power generation provided a minimum environmental flow was maintained.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct — the Permanent Court of Arbitration allowed India to proceed with the Kishanganga project. (R) is correct — the court stipulated that India must maintain a minimum flow of 9 cumecs downstream. (R) explains (A) because the permission was conditional on maintaining environmental flow, which was the basis of the ruling.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Salal Dam on the Chenab river in J&K has an installed capacity of:
questions.explanation: The Salal Hydroelectric Power Station on the Chenab has an installed capacity of 690 MW (6 × 115 MW). 390 MW is incorrect. 480 MW is the capacity of Uri-I on the Jhelum. 900 MW exceeds Salal's actual capacity.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Which of the following statements about the economic development of J&K vis-à-vis the Indus Waters Treaty are correct?

(i) The treaty has been a factor in J&K's power deficit situation.
(ii) Flood damage in the Kashmir Valley could be reduced with larger storage dams.
(iii) The treaty prohibits India from building any structure on western rivers.
(iv) Revenue from hydroelectric projects on western rivers contributes to J&K's economy.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — treaty restrictions contribute to J&K generating less power than its potential. (ii) is correct — storage dams could regulate flood waters, but their size is restricted. (iv) is correct — existing run-of-the-river projects like Salal, Uri, Baglihar generate revenue. (iii) is wrong — the treaty does NOT prohibit ALL structures; it allows run-of-the-river projects and limited storage.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: For over six decades after 1960 the Indus Waters Treaty continued to operate despite several India-Pakistan wars. Until 2025, this was most often cited as an example of:
options: Successful water-sharing cooperation between hostile nations
Complete resolution of all bilateral disputes
Dominance of one nation over another's water resources
questions.correctAnswer: Successful water-sharing cooperation between hostile nations
questions.explanation: Between 1960 and 2025 the treaty kept functioning through the wars of 1965, 1971 and 1999, and was therefore routinely cited as a rare instance of durable water-sharing cooperation between hostile neighbours. The framing must now be dated, because in April 2025, after the Pahalgam attack, India announced it was holding the treaty 'in abeyance'; in September 2026 the Court of Arbitration at The Hague held that the treaty remains in force and cannot be suspended unilaterally, an award India rejected while maintaining the abeyance. The other options are wrong because the treaty is a bilateral water-sharing arrangement brokered by the World Bank, not a military, trade or territorial settlement.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Under the Indus Waters Treaty the three western rivers allocated principally to Pakistan are the Indus, the Jhelum and the __________, all of which flow through J&K.
questions.explanation: The treaty splits the system into three eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — allocated to India, and three western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — allocated principally to Pakistan, with India retaining non-consumptive, limited-irrigation and run-of-the-river hydro rights on them. The Chenab is therefore the correct completion, and it carries J&K's largest hydel projects, Salal, Baglihar, Dulhasti and Ratle. Ravi, Beas and Sutlej are all wrong because each is an eastern river assigned to India, not a western one.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the Pakal Dul Hydroelectric Project:

(i) It is being built on the Marusudar river, a tributary of the Chenab.
(ii) It will be the largest hydroelectric project in J&K once completed.
(iii) It includes a concrete-face rock-fill dam.
(iv) Pakistan has raised no objections to this project.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — Pakal Dul is on the Marusudar river (Chenab tributary) in Kishtwar district. (ii) is correct — at 1,000 MW, it will be J&K's largest when completed. (iii) is correct — it features a concrete-face rock-fill dam (CFRD). (iv) is wrong — Pakistan has raised concerns about this project as it involves storage on a western river tributary.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The total number of rivers covered under the Indus Waters Treaty is:
questions.explanation: The treaty covers six rivers — three eastern (Sutlej, Beas, Ravi) and three western (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab). 'Three' counts only one group. 'Five' undercounts. 'Eight' overcounts and may confuse tributaries with main rivers.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): J&K has argued for a review or renegotiation of the Indus Waters Treaty.
Reason (R): The treaty was signed when J&K had limited autonomy and its interests regarding water resources were not adequately represented.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct — there have been persistent demands from J&K stakeholders for treaty renegotiation or amendment. (R) is correct — J&K was not a direct party to the negotiations in 1960, and its specific developmental interests were not fully represented. (R) explains (A) because the feeling of being inadequately represented is the core reason driving renegotiation demands.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Match the following hydroelectric projects with their installed capacities:

Column I:
(a) Uri-I
(b) Salal
(c) Dulhasti
(d) Baglihar (Stage I)

Column II:
(i) 390 MW
(ii) 480 MW
(iii) 450 MW
(iv) 690 MW

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Uri-I has 480 MW capacity (ii). Salal has 690 MW capacity (iv). Dulhasti has 390 MW capacity (i). Baglihar Stage-I has 450 MW capacity (iii). Option 1 incorrectly swaps Dulhasti and Baglihar capacities. Option 2 wrongly assigns 690 MW to Uri-I. Option 4 assigns 390 MW to Uri-I instead of Dulhasti.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Indus Waters Treaty allows India to generate how much hydroelectric power from the western rivers?
options: A fixed limit of 5,000 MW only
No hydroelectric power generation is allowed
Unlimited power generation through run-of-the-river projects (no storage limit applies to power)
Power generation is allowed but with design restrictions on dam height and pondage
questions.correctAnswer: Power generation is allowed but with design restrictions on dam height and pondage
questions.explanation: The treaty allows India to generate hydroelectric power from western rivers but imposes design restrictions on dam height, pondage (live storage), and spillway gates. There is no fixed MW limit of 5,000 MW. It is wrong that no power generation is allowed — run-of-the-river projects are clearly permitted. 'Unlimited without storage limits' is wrong because there ARE storage/pondage limits.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the Ratle Hydroelectric Project:

(i) It is located on the Chenab river in Kishtwar district.
(ii) Its planned capacity is 850 MW.
(iii) Pakistan has objected to this project under the treaty.
(iv) It is a storage-based project with no run-of-the-river component.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — Ratle is on the Chenab in Kishtwar district of J&K. (ii) is correct — the planned capacity is 850 MW. (iii) is correct — Pakistan has raised objections, seeking a Court of Arbitration. (iv) is wrong — Ratle is designed as a run-of-the-river project with limited pondage, not a large storage dam.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
The following data shows the installed capacity (in MW) of hydroelectric projects on western rivers in J&K:

Uri-I → Jhelum, 480
Uri-II → Jhelum, 240
Salal → Chenab, 690
Baglihar-I → Chenab, 450
Dulhasti → Chenab, 390

What is the total installed capacity of the projects on the Chenab river shown above?
questions.explanation: Chenab river projects: Salal (690) + Baglihar-I (450) + Dulhasti (390) = 1,530 MW. Option 1,140 MW omits one project. Option 1,770 MW incorrectly adds a Jhelum project. Option 2,250 MW adds all five projects together.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Which of the following is a major criticism of the Indus Waters Treaty from J&K's perspective?

(i) The treaty was a central government decision without J&K's consent.
(ii) It prevents optimal utilization of J&K's water resources for development.
(iii) It provides no compensation mechanism to J&K for foregone development.
(iv) All the rivers flowing through J&K are allocated entirely to Pakistan.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — J&K was not a party to the treaty negotiations. (ii) is correct — restrictions on storage prevent full utilization of river resources. (iii) is correct — there is no formal compensation framework for J&K. (iv) is wrong — the rivers are not allocated 'entirely' to Pakistan; India retains limited use rights, and existing projects like Uri and Salal operate on these rivers.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: The Wular Barrage (Tulbul Navigation Project) on the Jhelum was halted due to Pakistan's objection under the treaty. What was the project's intended purpose?
options: Large-scale irrigation for the entire Kashmir Valley
Navigation improvement and flood control on the Jhelum near Wular Lake
Complete diversion of the Jhelum for power generation
Drinking water supply to Srinagar city only
questions.correctAnswer: Navigation improvement and flood control on the Jhelum near Wular Lake
questions.explanation: The Tulbul Navigation Project was intended to improve navigation on the Jhelum and provide flood management near Wular Lake. It was not for 'large-scale irrigation' of the entire valley. It was not for 'complete diversion' — that would violate the treaty. It was not solely for 'drinking water to Srinagar' — it had broader purposes.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The Indus Waters Treaty has been called the 'most generous water treaty' by some Indian analysts.
Reason (R): India gave up rights over 80% of the Indus system's water (western rivers) to Pakistan despite being the upper riparian state.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct — many Indian analysts and politicians have described the treaty as overly generous to Pakistan. (R) is correct — approximately 80% of the total Indus water flow comes from the western rivers that were allocated to Pakistan, despite India being the upper riparian state. (R) explains (A) because giving up majority of the water as the upstream country is precisely why analysts call it generous.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
The following data shows the approximate hydroelectric potential and harnessed capacity for different river basins in J&K:

Chenab → 11,000, 1,530
Jhelum → 3,500, 720
Ravi → 2,000, 200
Indus → 3,500, 50

Which river basin has the lowest percentage of its potential harnessed?
questions.explanation: Percentages harnessed: Chenab = 1530/11000 = 13.9%, Jhelum = 720/3500 = 20.6%, Ravi = 200/2000 = 10%, Indus = 50/3500 = 1.4%. The Indus basin has the lowest percentage harnessed at just 1.4%. Ravi (10%) is second lowest. Chenab (13.9%) is third. Jhelum (20.6%) has the highest percentage harnessed.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText: Under the Indus Waters Treaty, the concept of 'pondage' refers to:
options: The total volume of water in all rivers
Temporary storage of water behind a dam to regulate daily or weekly flow for power generation
Permanent diversion of water from one river to another
The natural depth of the river at the dam site
questions.correctAnswer: Temporary storage of water behind a dam to regulate daily or weekly flow for power generation
questions.explanation: Pondage is the temporary storage of water behind a run-of-the-river dam to regulate flow variations for consistent power generation, not permanent large-scale storage. 'Total volume in all rivers' describes annual flow, not pondage. 'Permanent diversion' is something different entirely. 'Natural depth of river' describes river hydrology, not a dam feature.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Match the following disputed projects with the dispute resolution mechanism used:

Column I:
(a) Baglihar Dam
(b) Kishanganga Project
(c) Salal Dam
(d) Tulbul Navigation Project

Column II:
(i) Bilateral negotiations (resolved)
(ii) Neutral Expert
(iii) Court of Arbitration
(iv) Remained unresolved/stalled

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Baglihar went to a Neutral Expert (ii) — Professor Lafitte in 2005-07. Kishanganga went to the Permanent Court of Arbitration (iii) — decided in 2013. Salal was resolved through bilateral negotiations (i) — agreement reached in 1978. Tulbul (Wular Barrage) remains unresolved/stalled (iv) — India halted construction after Pakistan's objections and it hasn't resumed.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the economic potential of the Chenab river basin in J&K:

(i) The Chenab basin alone holds over 50% of J&K's total hydroelectric potential.
(ii) Several upcoming projects like Pakal Dul and Ratle will significantly increase power generation.
(iii) The basin supports agriculture in the Jammu division through canal systems.
(iv) The treaty completely bars any new project on the Chenab.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — the Chenab basin holds approximately 11,000 MW out of J&K's total ~20,000 MW potential (over 50%). (ii) is correct — Pakal Dul (1,000 MW) and Ratle (850 MW) are under development. (iii) is correct — canal networks from the Chenab irrigate areas in Jammu division. (iv) is wrong — the treaty does NOT bar new projects; it permits run-of-the-river projects with design restrictions.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
The following data shows the annual flow (in MAF) of the six Indus system rivers:

Indus → 93
Jhelum → 23
Chenab → 26
Ravi → 7
Beas → 13
Sutlej → 14

What percentage of total Indus system flow do the western rivers (allocated to Pakistan) constitute approximately?
questions.explanation: Western rivers flow = Indus (93) + Jhelum (23) + Chenab (26) = 142 MAF. Total flow = 142 + 7 + 13 + 14 = 176 MAF. Percentage = 142/176 × 100 ≈ 80.7% ≈ 80%. 60% undercounts the western river share. 70% is also too low. 90% overcounts.

questions.subject: C
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the current position of the Indus Waters Treaty:

(i) Climate change and glacial melt may alter water availability in the Indus system.
(ii) India placed the treaty in abeyance in April 2025, following the Pahalgam attack.
(iii) In September 2026 the Court of Arbitration at The Hague held that the treaty remains in force and cannot be suspended unilaterally.
(iv) The treaty contains a clause under which it automatically expires after sixty years.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — retreating glaciers and shifting precipitation are expected to change flows in the Indus system, a live concern for J&K's hydel planning. (ii) is correct — India announced the abeyance in April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack in which 26 people, mostly tourists, were killed. (iii) is correct — in September 2026 the Court of Arbitration at The Hague ruled that the treaty remains in force and recognises no status of 'abeyance'; India rejected the award, disputing the court's jurisdiction, and has maintained its position. (iv) is wrong — the treaty has no expiry date and continues until both parties replace it by a duly ratified treaty, so every option containing (iv) is incorrect.
